1:
The chapter opens by answering a complaint. Charles Ellicott says the declaration answers the murmur of the previous chapter, that the glorious promises had not yet been fulfilled, and that the murmurers are told the hindrance is on their side. Matthew Henry reads it as the prophet rectifying a mistake in those quarrelling with God because the deliverances they had prayed for were not granted; they had no reason to lay the fault on him. He takes the two clauses as two answers. God is still as able to help as ever, his power neither lessened nor abridged; neither length of time nor strength of enemies nor weakness of instruments can shorten it, and with him it is one to save by many or by few. And he is still as ready to help, since his ear is not heavy: though he has many prayers to hear and has been long hearing prayer, he is as ready as ever, the prayer of the upright being as much his delight and the promises pleaded in prayer still inviolably sure. John Gill reads the same words of a later age, that it is not for want of power that God has not yet destroyed the enemies of his people or brought on the glorious state of the church, his hand being as long as ever.

Adam Clarke sets out the chapter’s plan. The previous chapter reproved the people for hypocrisy in fasting without true repentance while they still oppressed the poor; this one contains a more general reproof of their wickedness, bloodshed, violence and injustice, after which they make an ample confession of their sins, and on that act of humiliation a promise is given that the Redeemer will come like a mighty hero, destroy his enemies and give a new and everlasting covenant. Clarke also praises the composition: the chapter is remarkable for the beauty and variety of its images, and peculiarly distinguished by the exact construction of its sentences, falling regularly into stanzas of four lines from the first verse to the last two.

The cause of the silence is named in the second verse, and the figure used for it is agreed. Ellicott says the iniquities have become as it were a middle wall of partition excluding them from the divine presence, and Gill uses the same image; he applies it to the reformed churches of his own day, which profess the true God and attend the outward ordinances but so coldly and formally, with such wickedness connived at, that God stands at a distance from them. Two textual points attach to the same verse. Ellicott prefers the face to his face, since the Hebrew has neither article nor possessive pronoun; Clarke reports the same reading from several ancient versions, and adds a scholar’s note that the singular should perhaps be read because God is the speaker, though Clarke himself thinks the divine speech closed with the previous chapter and that this one is delivered in the person of the prophet.

Particulars begin with the hands. Ellicott notes that the accusation reproduces verbatim the indictment of the book’s opening chapter. Keil and Delitzsch classify the list as sins in words and deeds, and attend to the grammar: the verb meaning to spot is a later softening of an older form, and the participle here is a double passive compounded of two conjugations; the verb rendered mutter, they add, combines the meanings of reflection and of a light low expression, half inward and half outward. Gill observes that idolatry is not mentioned, which an earlier father took to show that the prophecy belongs to other times than the prophet’s own; and he reads the shedding of blood as covering murder, wars, persecutions, and at least the want of brotherly love, which is itself called murder. Clarke notes that an ancient manuscript and two versions add a conjunction before the tongue.
4:
The indictment moves from words to the courts. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition to social and judicial life, where lying and oppression universally prevail, and render the clause no one speaks with justice and no one pleads with faithfulness. They defend that rendering against a judicial one, since the verb is generally used in these addresses in the sense of proclaiming, so that the meaning is that no one gives public evidence with justice; and they define the terms—firm adherence to the rule of right and truth, and a conscientious reliance that awakens trust. Charles Ellicott prefers none preferreth his suit with truthfulness, taking the words to point chiefly at the guilt of unrighteous prosecutions though they may include false witness; he notes that the word rendered vanity is literally chaos, the characteristic term of both parts of the book. John Gill reads the calling for righteousness in an evangelical rather than a civil sense, that few preach the righteousness which is the grand doctrine of the gospel and few hunger to hear it, choosing instead the doctrine of justification by works. John Wesley keeps to the plain civil sense, that none seek to redress these wrongs and violences, so that rapine and fraud are committed with impunity. Adam Clarke admires the last figure, finding a curious propriety in comparing a purpose to conception and the act following it to the birth of a child, and holds that from the third verse to the fifteenth we have a true statement of the moral state of the people.

The two images that follow are read as a pair. Ellicott explains their logic: the schemes of the evil-doers are displayed in their power for evil and their impotence for good—to eat of the eggs, assumed to be poisonous, is to fall in with their schemes and be ruined, while to crush them is to oppose and so rouse a more venomous opposition, since men break the egg and the living viper darts out to attack them. Wesley treats both as proverbial, one venomous creature put for any, the eggs signifying mischievous designs and the hatching their being put into practice; and the web teaching two things at once, how by their plots they weave nets and lay snares with great pains and artifice, and how their designs will come to nothing, as a spider’s web is soon swept away. Ellicott makes the same double point about the web, that the comparison lies chiefly in its uselessness but that the second clause emphasises the only purpose it serves being one of mischief—webs may catch flies, they cannot clothe men. Gill applies both figures to false doctrine: invented teachings may look plausible as the eggs look fit to eat, but are poisonous; and schemes spun out of men’s own brains are as thin as a web, unable to stand before the word of God, which sweeps them away. He presses the second further: such webs are too thin to cover a naked body, and so cannot cover the nakedness of a sinner in the sight of God or screen him from avenging justice. Wesley says the same in a line, that their contrivances shall not be able to cover or defend them. Keil and Delitzsch carry the description on to its climax, that this evil-doing rises even to hatred, the very opposite of the love well-pleasing to God, and note that the Apostle wove the passage about running feet into his own description of the universal corruption of morals; they observe that the comparison of life to a road and of conduct to walking is common in proverbial sayings, from which the prophet took both his simile and his expressions.
7:
The picture of running feet and crooked paths is drawn almost entirely from the road. Charles Ellicott notes the parallelisms, entirely after this prophet’s manner, with the book of Proverbs, and observes that the four words for paths and goings and ways all come from that book. John Gill takes the running as making haste to commit all manner of sin with eagerness and swiftness, taking delight in it and continuing in it as a course of life, and notes that the words are quoted with what follows by the Apostle to prove the general corruption of mankind. John Wesley reads the wasting as what they meditate on and little else, and the paths as meaning that in whatever work they are engaged it all tends to ruin. Keil and Delitzsch take the figure further into the vocabulary, distinguishing the words used interchangeably—the way a man goes, the high-road thrown up with an embankment, the carriage-road, and the footpath formed by the constant passing of travellers. Their whole nature, they say, is broken up into discord: peaceable conduct springing from a love of peace is altogether strange to them, no recognition or practice of right is met with in their path, they make their paths diligently twisting about, and whoever treads on them forfeits all peace inward or outward. They observe that the word for peace is repeated significantly at the end, in this prophet’s peculiar style. Gill lists the several senses of the peace they do not know—peace with God, peace of conscience, eternal peace, and peace among men, which they are unconcerned about and take no methods to promote. Wesley says the same in a line, that they live in continual contentions and discords with no justice or integrity. Adam Clarke attends only to the grammar of the last clause, proposing that a singular pronoun be read as plural on the authority of four ancient versions, or else that a plural noun be read as singular as one ancient manuscript has it, in order to preserve the concord.

At the ninth verse the speaker changes, and this is the turn on which the chapter hinges. Keil and Delitzsch describe a second strophe in which the prophet includes himself when speaking of the people: they mourn over the exhaustion brought on by the perpetual straining and disappointment of expectation, and confess the sins for which righteousness and salvation have been withheld. He speaks communicatively, they explain, because even the better portion of the nation was involved in the guilt and consequences of the prevailing corruption, a nation forming an organised whole. Matthew Henry sets out the same shift as a change of speaker rather than of subject. The scope of the paragraph is the same as the last, to show that sin is the great mischief-maker; but where that was spoken by the prophet in God’s name to the people, this seems spoken by the people to God, as an acknowledgement of what had been told them and a submission to the justice of his proceedings. Their uncircumcised hearts seem in some measure humbled, and they are brought to confess—the confession, he says, being at least extorted from them—that God had justly walked contrary to them because they had walked contrary to him. Henry hears them acknowledging their case: they are trampled on and ruled with rigour, and God does not appear to plead their injured cause; though against their persecutors they are sure that right is on their side, they are not righted, because they had not done justice to one another and God therefore suffers their enemies to deal unjustly with them. Gill identifies the speakers more narrowly as the few godly persons of those times, taking notice of the prevailing sins, confessing and lamenting them, and observing that these were the source of the calamities under which they groaned.
10:
The confession begins with images of blindness and animal noise. John Gill describes the groping literally, of those who with their hands or a staff feel for the wall to lean against or to guide them into the house, so that they may know whereabouts they are. Charles Ellicott notes a striking parallelism with the curses of Deuteronomy, which the words may have been reproduced from or in. On the last clause of the verse he reports that many critics render it not in desolate places but among those full of life, or in luxuriant fields, and prefers the first of these as giving an antithesis like that of the other clauses. John Wesley takes the same clause of the captivity, comparing it to men dead without hope of recovery. Adam Clarke attends to a repetition in the verse which he thinks unworthy of the prophet: the same verb for groping occurs twice, and he adopts an emendation replacing the second with a verb meaning to stumble, calling the repetition poor and inelegant and unlike this writer’s manner. The mistake, he says, is of long standing, being prior to all the ancient versions, and was very easy and obvious, so that he has little doubt the true reading has been recovered.

The two creatures named in the next verse are chosen for the contrast between them. Gill sets it out: some mourn in a noisy and clamorous way and others in a stiller one, yet all in private, since the bear robbed of its whelps goes to its den and roars while the dove that has lost its mate mourns in solitude; this, he says, expresses the secret groanings of the faithful under a sense of sin and the forlorn state of religion. Wesley draws the same line differently, that their oppressing governors made the wicked roar like bears and the good mourn like doves. Ellicott observes that the comparison with bears is not found elsewhere in Scripture, though a Roman poet has the bear moaning round the sheepfold, and refers the dove to two other passages. Clarke notes that a conjunction must necessarily be prefixed to the verb in the last clause, as three ancient versions found it in their copies.

Keil and Delitzsch explain how the section is put together. The people had already indicated that this benighted and hopeless state was the consequence of their prevailing sins, and now come back to that and strike the note of penitence, which is easily recognised by the recurring rhymes at the ends of the verbs; the prophet makes the confession standing at the head of the people as the leader of their prayer. Ellicott finds the parallelism with the confessions of Daniel and Ezra singularly striking, and observes that this is as explicable on the supposition that they reproduced this passage as on the assumption that this too was written at the close of the exile, since the words would be as true in the time of Manasseh as at any later period; the self-accusations of the people, he adds, are now as full and severe as the prophet’s original indictment had been. Gill notes that the increase of transgression is not only among the people in common but among professors of religion, and that being committed against the Lord they are observed by him and call aloud for judgment. Wesley presses the particular word used, which he says signifies sins of a high kind, in which there is much of man’s will against light; they admit of no excuse, being acted before God and multiplied against him, the sins testifying like so many witnesses produced to prove their guilt, still unforgiven and fully known to those who confess them.
13:
The list of transgressions is analysed into parts. Charles Ellicott takes the clauses to point to false and hypocritical worship, to open apostasy, and to sins against man, the last subdivided into sins against truth and against justice. John Wesley pairs the first two words, since in transgressing the law they broke their solemn engagement made at Sinai, and reads the departing as turning from God to idols; the speaking he takes to mean they talked of little else but how to oppress their neighbours, and the uttering to mean contriving false accusations in the heart and then bringing them out—when they dealt with men by fraud it was from the heart, but when they spoke with God it was only from the lip. John Gill refers the lying to the word of the Lord and applies it to the denial of Christ’s deity, which he says is notorious in his own day.

The confession then turns from personal sins to the state of society. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition and warn against a misreading: the two words here are not the manifestation of divine judgment and justice prevented from being realised, but the people continuing to confess their own moral depravity. Right has been forced back from the place it ought to occupy—the verb being that used in the law for removing boundaries—and righteousness looks on from afar at the unjust habits of the people without being able to interpose. Gill agrees that the passage concerns the want of judgment among men, though he notes that one Jewish commentator took it the other way. Ellicott locates the scene: truth falls in the broad open place or market of the city, words which point naturally to Jerusalem, so that if they refer to Babylon we must assume the exiles had a quarter of their own with a market for business and judicial proceedings. Wesley takes the whole verse of the courts, where truth is cast to the ground and justice trampled underfoot even in public, and no equity is admitted. Adam Clarke reports a gloss on the word for righteousness, that a Jewish commentator understood it of alms to the poor, and observes that this casts light on a disputed reading in the Gospel, where the better copies have righteousness and the word for alms seems to have entered as an explanation.

The fifteenth verse is read as the hinge of the chapter. Gill takes the failing of truth as its being deprived of life, so that it seems to have expired, error prevailing until truth springs up again. Ellicott glosses it as truth banished and become a lost thing, and gives two other renderings of the following clause—that the man who departs from evil is outlawed, or counted mad—while holding the received version tenable, and finds the words reminiscent of an ancient historian’s picture of a demoralised society. Wesley gives the same alternatives, and cites a historian’s report that immediately before the destruction of Jerusalem it was matter of scorn to be religious; the received word means that the wicked like wild beasts devour those who are not as bad as themselves. On what it was that the Lord saw, Ellicott resists the first impression. The verse at first suggests that he saw the sins just described, but the sequence of thought tends rather to make these words the beginning of a new section, the supplied pronoun referring to the repentance and confession of the people: what displeased him was that the penitents were still subject to oppression and found no leader or deliverer, and therefore he came alone and unaided to the rescue. Clarke thinks the line defective and supplies a lost phrase, conjecturing that it originally read that the Lord saw it and was wroth, and that it displeased him that there was no judgment—an omission, if it is one, older than all the versions.
16:
The turn from indictment to deliverance is the subject here, and Matthew Henry puts it as a contrast of measures. How sin abounded we have read in the former part of the chapter; how grace does much more abound we read in these verses; and as sin took occasion from the commandment to become more sinful, so grace took occasion from the transgression to appear more gracious. He asks why God wrought salvation for so provoking a people, and answers that it was for his own name’s sake, since in them was no merit to deserve it and no might to effect it. Henry sets out what God saw: no man who would do anything for the bleeding cause of religion, none who would bestir himself in a work of reformation; those who complained of the times had not zeal enough to act, so that corruption was universal with nothing done to stem the tide, most being wicked and the rest too weak to attempt anything. And there was no intercessor—none to stand in the gap by prayer and turn away his wrath, which it would have pleased him to be met with, or rather none to interpose for justice and truth. John Gill qualifies it: not that there was no such person, but comparatively none, since the previous verse had mentioned some who departed from evil and made themselves a prey. Charles Ellicott notes that if the words mean no righteous man there is a parallel elsewhere, and that the intercessor points to the action of the two men who stayed a plague; on his own reading, no man means no champion. John Wesley reads it the same way: none appeared on behalf of equity, so God would do his work without help and avenge the innocent himself.

Adam Clarke reports that some rabbinic authorities understood these verses of the Messiah, and quotes one who set two prophecies against each other—that he will come in the clouds of heaven, and that he comes lowly riding on an ass—reconciling them by saying that if the people have merit he will come in the clouds, and if not, on the ass. Clarke turns the answer against those who gave it; the dilemma is reported here, not that use of it.

The armour is described piece by piece. Gill takes the whole as a picture of a warrior, and reads the breastplate as securing God’s faithfulness and justice in saving his people and destroying their enemies, the honour of his name preserved as the breast is by the breastplate. Wesley reads the same piece as showing the justness of God’s cause and his faithfulness in his promises, and divides the armour by purpose: the first pieces are put on for those he would preserve, the garments of vengeance for those he would destroy; the expressions describe cause and effect together, the cause righteousness and zeal in God, the effect salvation to his people and vengeance on his enemies. Clarke draws the same division: a breastplate and helmet to bring righteousness and salvation to those who fear him, the garments of vengeance and the cloak of zeal for the destruction of those who oppose him. He also argues that one word in the verse is an interpolation on five grounds: it is in no ancient version, it is redundant, it makes the half-line longer than the others adjoining, it makes the construction less elegant, and it may have stood in a margin as a variant and been taken into the text. Ellicott identifies the garments as the short tunic hanging over the breastplate and the scarlet mantle of a soldier, whose colour probably made it a symbol of zeal, and notes that the parallelism with an earlier chapter points as far as it goes to identity of authorship, while the parallel with the Apostle’s whole armour of God gives that passage new significance.
18:
The verse announcing repayment is corrupt or at best obscure. Adam Clarke says the former part as it stands in the Hebrew seems to him very imperfect and absolutely unintelligible. He reports that a learned commentator laboured over it, following one earlier interpreter he thought the only one to have understood it at all; between them the sense had been clearly made out, but Clarke does not expect a third person to be of that opinion. He gives the rendering arrived at—according to the height of their demerits he will repay them to the height, fury to his adversaries, recompense to his enemies—and remarks that those who hold the Hebrew text infallible must make their way through it as they can, but ought to give us something with the appearance of sense. He does not think the case desperate: an ancient version leads fairly to a correction, reading the Lord of retribution, he will render recompense, which supposes one letter different from the received text. John Wesley takes the first noun as recompenses or deserts, so that God repays his adversaries with the effects of his fury that they have deserved, and reads the islands as remoter nations that thought themselves secure. Charles Ellicott makes the judgment general against all, within Israel or outside it, who come under the description, takes islands in its usual sense of far-off lands, and says the words point to every such judgment from that of Cyrus to the great final day. John Gill reads it as the law of retribution—as the enemies of God’s people have treated them, so will he deal with them—and applies it to the ecclesiastical power he takes for the antichrist of the Revelation, to whom double is to be rendered according to her works.

The nineteenth verse divides the commentators twice over. On its first half Gill reads the fear of the name from west and east as the spread of the gospel in both directions once the antichristian powers are destroyed, so that God is served by all nations under heaven and even those who escape the general ruin are frightened at his judgments; Wesley glosses the two directions simply as the western and eastern parts of the world. On its second half the difficulty is grammatical. Ellicott lists the senses the noun admits—adversary, adversity, hemmed in, rushing—and gives two of the renderings that have followed from them: that the Lord shall come like a rushing stream which his own breath drives, or that adversity shall come like a stream. He calls the verse difficult but holds the received version at least as tenable as any other, finding parallels for the flood in one prophet and for the banner in a psalm. Clarke prefers one of the alternatives, translating the clause as which a strong wind driveth along, and supports it from the Latin version; he reports that a Jewish commentator’s father derived the verb from a root meaning to put to flight, giving the sense that the Spirit of the Lord shall put the enemy to flight, though Clarke explains the action otherwise, and notes that a conjunction seems necessary before the word for spirit and is added by a corrector in one manuscript. Clarke also reports that the rabbinic authorities referred the verse to the coming of the Messiah, with the rule that if you see a generation enduring much tribulation you may expect him; and he passes on an explanation of the standard, that the standard-bearer always began the battle by striking the first blow, so that here the Spirit of the Lord strikes first—those who go against sin with the Holy Spirit at their head being sure to win the day. Wesley reads the same clause as the promise that whenever violent irruptions are made on the church, God will make himself known to take their part and defend them by his Spirit alone.
20:
The Redeemer promised at the close is identified almost unanimously. John Gill rejects the view that Cyrus is meant and applies the words to the Messiah, as the Jewish authorities he cites do, adding that one of them understood the enemy of the preceding verse as the last hostile powers; he takes the coming here not of the first advent to redeem by blood but of a spiritual coming to the church in the latter day, at the conversion of the Jews, as the Apostle’s use of the passage suggests. John Wesley reads it the same way, that the Redeemer is Christ, and observes that the prophets usually conclude their promises of temporal deliverance with promises of spiritual deliverance, of which the temporal were evident types. Charles Ellicott keeps the figure of the whole passage running, that the picture of the divine appearing is continued and the Lord comes as a kinsman-redeemer to the true Zion, to those who have turned from their transgression; he notes that the verse is quoted with variations by the Apostle.

Those variations are the chapter’s last textual question. Adam Clarke observes that the Greek version and the Apostle read the clause as a promise that God shall turn away iniquity from Jacob, rather than that the Redeemer shall come to those who turn from transgression in Jacob, and shows how the difference arises from two words being read otherwise than in the received text; the Syriac agrees with the Greek and the Chaldee gives the same sense, while the received translation expresses the present reading of the Hebrew. He notes a second variant in the following verse, where twenty-four manuscripts and nine editions read with them for them.

The covenant that closes the chapter is read as new in the strict sense. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the opening words are a renewal of what God said to Abram, with the same form of expression, and that having come as a Redeemer to a people hitherto lying under the curse he now makes an everlasting covenant with them. Ellicott says the same of the form and goes further as to the substance: the words are the germ of the promise of a new covenant developed by a later prophet and taken up in the Epistle, and the new covenant is to involve the gift of the Spirit that writes the law of God inwardly in the heart, as distinct from the Law, which is thought of as outside the conscience, doing its work as an accuser and a judge. Clarke takes the address as spoken to the Messiah, though he reports a Jewish commentator’s view that it is spoken to the prophet, informing him that the spirit of prophecy would be given to all Israelites in the days of the Messiah as it was then given to him. He draws out the succession the verse promises: whatever Christ spoke was the word and mind of God and must be implicitly received; the same doctrines he preached, all his faithful ministers preach; and those born of God believe them, so that the doctrines remain in the seed’s seed through all generations. Gill limits the application to those to whom the covenant is manifested and made good, who repent of their sins and believe, and to whom its particular blessing of forgiveness is applied.
